summary:
Çankırı province stands under the national framework of Turkey, which presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations of the right to liberty in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — and 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51. The organisation's assessment is that hostility became explicit state policy in 2025, driven by "Year of the Family" instructions from senior officials and directed at public institutions.

A leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend penal-code article 225 to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years in prison, and would allow charges against anyone taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony, carrying up to four years. Under civil-code article 40 the same package would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 and impose a permanent-infertility mandate, exposing providers to fines and up to seven years and patients to up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected, and Human Rights Watch has called for withdrawal. The measure had not been passed when reported, but authorities have acted as though the prohibitions were already in force.

That gap between text and practice is visible in street-level enforcement. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release; legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women stated that no fines were issued but that she was documented anyway, and that enforcement was already being applied to her before any new law had passed. Foreign nationals stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents, and Turkey requires foreigners to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, every checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is asymmetric. Kaos GL documented six right-to-life violations in 2025, three of them hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected group. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary basis, transfers disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, risking the profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to care.

Çankırı is assessed relative to this national picture as the most conservative province near the capital. Neither source reviewed records province-specific enforcement or incidents here; the findings above describe the framework the province sits inside, not documented events within it.
tangentialFactors:
The state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so the counts in the Kaos GL 2025 report rest on media coverage rather than administrative records. Undercounting is therefore a standing possibility, and the direction of the error is unlikely to be toward overstatement.

The draft judicial package was still pending when Human Rights Watch reported it on 29 October 2025, yet the conduct it would criminalise was already being enforced against trans women in Istanbul. Pending legislation in Turkey has functioned as operative instruction rather than as a proposal awaiting a vote.

Objection to the package came from inside Turkish professional life as well as from advocacy organisations: fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed it, and Human Rights Watch called for withdrawal. The medical association's position matters for a trans visitor considering care in Turkey, since the profession's own representative body is on record against the proposed restrictions.

The pattern has depth beyond the current cycle. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's continuity, not as a statement of current law.
localsOnly:
Residents face the same penal-code exposure as visitors under the draft 11th Judicial Package, with the age rise for gender-affirming care and the permanent-infertility mandate falling on them directly: providers would face fines and up to seven years, patients up to three years.

Transition care administration has been tightened at national level. The Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, building on a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that listed "gender reassignment" among official reasons for medical-board reports, removed the "other" option from hospital records and required e-reports, which places trans patients' status in searchable official documentation.

Trans prisoners are assigned by registered sex. The death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025, the delayed medical and forensic response, the absence of witness statements, and the parliamentary intervention by Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025 show that placement and custody conditions for trans inmates were under formal dispute through the end of 2025.

Detention for LGBT residents is routine rather than exceptional: Kaos GL counted 313 right-to-liberty violations and 89 torture or ill-treatment violations in 2025, and complaints mechanism are ineffective and can expose the complainant to further violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records enforcement actions, arrests, violence or facilities data specific to Çankırı. The province-level assessment is an inference from the national framework and from its characterization as the most conservative province near the capital, and it remains unverified against local reporting.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted is unresolved here. Human Rights Watch described it as a leaked draft pending before the government as of 29 October 2025; no later status is sourced, so its current legal standing is not established.

The claim that enforcement has proceeded ahead of legislation rests on reporting from Istanbul. Whether comparable document checks or detentions occur in Çankırı is not sourced either way.

The Kaos GL figures depend on media monitoring in the absence of official hate-crime statistics, so the true totals for 2025 are not independently verifiable from this inventory.
